title: What Does a UV Light Do in an HVAC System?
h1: What Does a UV Light Do in an HVAC System?
description: A UV light in your HVAC system keeps the coil free of mold and biological growth. Learn how HVAC UV lights work, their limits and who benefits most.
quick_answer: A UV light in an HVAC system uses ultraviolet light to keep mold, bacteria and other biological growth from building up inside the equipment, mainly on the evaporator coil and drain pan. Some models also treat moving air. UV lights don't remove dust, pollen or smoke, so they work alongside a good filter, not instead of one.
body:
The evaporator coil inside your system is cold and wet whenever the AC runs. That makes it a natural place for mold and bacteria to grow. A UV light shines on that area to keep growth from taking hold, which helps keep the coil clean and the air smelling fresh.

How does a UV light work in an HVAC system?

Ultraviolet light in the UV-C range damages the genetic material of microorganisms so they can't reproduce. The light is installed inside the air handler or ductwork, where it shines continuously on surfaces or into the airstream. The bulb is sealed away from view, since direct UV exposure can harm eyes and skin.

What types of HVAC UV lights are there?

  • Coil sterilization lights. These are mounted near the evaporator coil and stay on all the time. Because the coil and drain pan are exposed around the clock, this type is effective at keeping those surfaces clean.
  • Air sterilization lights. These are installed in the ductwork or return to treat air as it passes by. Air moves quickly, so each particle gets only a brief exposure. They're usually more useful as part of a larger air cleaning setup.

Some UV lights are designed to produce small amounts of ozone, which some people want to avoid. Ask what type you're getting, and look for models that don't produce ozone if that's a concern.

What are the benefits of a UV light?

  • Cleaner coil. Biological growth on the coil acts like insulation and restricts airflow. Keeping it clean helps the system perform as designed.
  • Fewer musty odors. Many dirty-sock smells come from growth on the coil and pan.
  • Less slime in the drain. A cleaner pan can mean fewer drain clogs.
  • Help for allergy-prone households. Keeping mold off the coil means less to circulate through the house.

What can't a UV light do?

UV light is good at one job, and it's easy to expect too much from it. It does not:

  • Trap dust, pollen, pet dander or smoke particles
  • Remove dust that's already on the coil or in the ducts
  • Fix a humidity problem or a clogged drain
  • Reach surfaces that are shaded from the bulb

That's why a UV light is paired with a good filter. If you're dealing with smoke or allergies, filtration and possibly an air purifier do most of the work. Our indoor air quality services can combine these based on what's going on in your home.

Who benefits most from a UV light?

A UV light makes the most sense if:

  1. Your system has had mold on the coil or in the drain pan before
  2. You notice a musty smell when the AC starts
  3. You live near the coast, where damp air keeps the coil wet longer
  4. Someone in the home has allergies or asthma
  5. Your drain line clogs with slime repeatedly

If your system is clean and dry and nobody has symptoms, a UV light is a nice extra rather than a must.

Where is a UV light installed?

In most homes here, the furnace or air handler sits in the attic, the garage or a hall closet. A coil light is mounted through a small opening in the cabinet or the duct right above the coil, so the bulb faces the coil surface and the drain pan. It's wired to a constant power source in the equipment, so it stays on even when the system isn't running.

Placement matters. A bulb that's too far away or shaded by parts won't reach the surfaces that need it, and UV can break down some plastics and wire insulation if it shines on them over time. That's one reason it's worth having it installed by someone who knows your equipment.

How do you maintain a UV light?

UV bulbs lose strength over time, even when they still glow. Most manufacturers recommend replacing the bulb about once a year, but check the instructions for your model. Bulbs also collect dust, which blocks the light, so they should be wiped during maintenance.

Always turn off power before the bulb is serviced, and never look directly at a lit UV bulb. Many people have the bulb checked and replaced during their yearly HVAC tune-up.
faqs: Yes, when they're installed inside the equipment where nobody can look at them. Direct UV-C exposure can hurt eyes and skin, so the power should be off before anyone opens the panel.
Do HVAC UV lights kill viruses in the air?

UV-C can inactivate many microorganisms on surfaces it reaches, but how much it reduces airborne germs in a home depends on the design and the time air spends near the light. It shouldn't be relied on as the only protection.
Will a UV light lower my energy bills?
A clean coil transfers heat better than a dirty one, which helps the system run as designed. But savings depend on how dirty the coil would otherwise get, so don't buy one for energy savings alone.
Can I install an HVAC UV light myself?

Most require wiring into the equipment's power and opening the air handler or ducts. Professional installation makes sure the bulb is placed correctly, wired safely and doesn't shine on parts that UV can damage.
